name: Hanukkah (Festival of Lights)
description: The rededication of the Temple after the Maccabean revolt. The light that conquers darkness.
biblicalBasis: 1 Maccabees 4:36-59 and 2 Maccabees 10:1-8 regarding the rededication of the Temple after its desecration by Antiochus IV Epiphanes. The Temple is cleansed, a new altar is built, and the celebration lasts eight days. According to Talmudic tradition (Shabbat 21b), they found only one jar of consecrated oil sealed with the high priest's seal—enough for one day, but it burned for eight days. Jesus in the Temple during Hanukkah: "Are you the Messiah, tell us plainly" (John 10:22-23).
significance: Hanukkah celebrates resilience of faith: a small group stands firm against an empire that seeks to force them to abandon their beliefs. The miracle of the oil testifies that God stretches the little until it is enough. The light kindled in darkness—one more each day—is a powerful image of hope growing. That Jesus was in the Temple during Hanukkah and confronted with the question of whether He is the Messiah gives the Festival of Lights Christological depth.
liturgicalContext: Celebrated on 25 Kislev for eight days. The hanukkiah, a nine-branched menorah, is lit: the shamash (servant candle) and one new light each evening. Levivot (potato latkes) and sufganiyot (donuts) are fried in oil. Dreidel games. The Al Hanissim prayer is added to the daily prayers.
history: The Maccabean revolt (167-164 BC) was a reaction against Antiochus IV, who banned Jewish religious practice and erected an altar to Zeus in the Temple. Judas Maccabeus led the revolt. The miracle of the oil is not mentioned in the Books of Maccabees but in the Talmud (2nd-5th centuries). Hanukkah is the only major Jewish holiday without a biblical (canonical) basis in the Hebrew Bible.
otConnections: Daniel 8 and 11 concerning "the abomination that causes desolation"—Antiochus's desecration of the Temple, which Daniel prophesied about. 1 Kings 8—the dedication of Solomon's Temple as a model. Haggai 2:1-9 on the glory of the rebuilt Temple. Jesus quotes "the abomination that causes desolation" from Daniel in his discourse on the end times (Matthew 24:15).
